fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Freedom Recast as Franchise", "body": "Clint opens by refusing the label of free man, calling himself a fellow slave who has worked out the system of law that governs everyone who takes part in it. He argues that in legal language freedom is defined as franchise, comparing a citizen to a McDonald's outlet run under a parent corporation, and describes the United States as a municipal corporation separate from the fifty states. The more free people believe they are, he says, the more they trust voting and democracy. Chance returns to this in his closing, asking how government can license people to do what none of them has the right to do in nature."}, {"title": "Birth Certificate, Person and Mask", "body": "Clint traces what he calls the voluntary slavery of modern citizenship back to the birth certificate. In his reading, delivery means abandonment, so parents surrender their property rights in the child, who becomes a ward of the state with the United States as domicile. He says over 140 countries share an international Social Security system that keeps everyone in contract. The footprint stamped onto the certificate and the word identity, heard as id entity, come up as symbols of the same trade. The result, Clint argues, is a person, which he says simply means status, and he notes that persona is Latin for mask."}, {"title": "A Law Book Behind the Religion", "body": "Clint says he once despised the Bible until he found references to it in legal texts, and he now argues it is a book of law rather than a religion, with religion built around it. He asks why the Bible has been treated as common law in Pennsylvania and England, recommends the 1828 Webster's dictionary for its scriptural citations, and contends that church and courtroom keep people from the language. He describes the first rule of slavery as never teaching a slave your language, which he ties to legal terms of art, meaning anything not of nature. Chance frames all this beforehand, asking literalists and atheists alike to stay open."}, {"title": "Money, Mammon and Living in Fiction", "body": "Identity, Clint argues, means sameness, and every name, address and number offered to prove it ties a person to something that does not exist in nature. He calls money fiction with no intrinsic value, and reads mammon as pricing a tree, livestock or a man as a commodity instead of valuing it as a self-evident part of existence, which is why no one can have two gods. Chance adds that dictionary breaks into diction and Ares, the god of war, casting commerce as a state of war, and Clint recalls a line that a civil war is a war over words."}, {"title": "Jehovah Restored as a Verb", "body": "Chance sets this up in his opening, asking listeners to hear God as nature and the forces of the cosmos rather than anything supernatural. Clint then says the name Jehovah appeared in scripture more than 6,000 times before later Bibles swapped it for lord, king and God. He argues god is a generic title for any magistrate or status that gives orders, and says older court records addressed judges as gods. Reading the 1828 Webster's entry, which says the name denotes permanent being, to be fixed, to stand or to abide, he concludes Jehovah is a verb: existence itself, everything self-evident and not created by man."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The living soul known as clint > richardson is a researcher of Natural Law, and is the author of a book called Strawman: The Real Story of Your Artificial Person. This massive tome tells the story of how legal fictions are used to control real people, through the wordplay of legalese. In this show, clint explains why he sees the Bible as foundational to the legal systems of western nations, the difference between natural law and legality, and much more. The truth is stranger than fiction.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Bible Read as Allegory", "body": "Chance opens the second hour with Lord of the Rings, and Clint asks why listeners happily treat Tolkien, The Odyssey and The Iliad as teaching stories yet insist on reading the Bible literally. He points to Jonah and the sea monster, a creature sailors once drew on maps, as proof that the text works through metaphor, aphorism and verse. Clint describes Tolkien as a naturalist who saw the spiritual battle between what man invents and what already exists, and argues that reading any of these tales literally, disbelieving in Mordor or Gandalf, would make a reader look foolish."}, {"title": "Nouns, Names and the Nameless", "body": "Chance reads a passage from The Straw Man Story on namelessness, and Clint builds on it with his theory that nouns were invented to put a mask over verbs and adjectives. In his reading a noun is a person, place or thing, which he maps onto status, jurisdiction and chattel property, while a verb simply acknowledges that something exists. He says nothing in nature has a name, calls sin a word tied to the synthetic, and claims legal usage defines a matrix as the first document showing existence, which in his view makes the birth certificate the matrix itself."}, {"title": "Two Kinds of Property", "body": "Chance asks Clint to explain the insight that first struck him, that property can mean something legally owned or an expression of something greater. Clint answers with chemistry: oxygen and hydrogen are properties of water, owned by nobody, while legal property is a movable thing that can be sold. He contrasts unalienable with inalienable, argues that labor has been turned into a commodity, and describes federal land as reserved for citizens. Chance adds the papal bulls posted on church doors, and Clint reads the Vicar of Christ entry to argue that antichrist simply means a replacement."}, {"title": "Existence, Insurance and Simulation", "body": "Clint argues that Jehovah was never meant to be debated because, as he recalls from the old Webster's, the name denotes something fixed, standing and permanent, the same sense he finds under the word exist. He uses insurance as his example: an act of God clause, defined in Black's Law as the exclusive operation of the forces of nature, shows in his view that the system itself recognizes a higher power. From there he calls atheism a disbelief in the existence of existence, and reports that looking up simulation in the old dictionary returned hypocrisy, which he treats as the true definition of the matrix."}, {"title": "Free Will, Parables and The Matrix", "body": "Clint says Christ always answered strangers in parable, offering a wise path and a foolish one rather than advice, so the listener kept free will. He argues most people do not want freedom because it means total responsibility and no insurance. Chance brings up the street preacher in They Live, and the pair tie Nada and Neo's refusal to the power of saying no. Clint claims the original Matrix script had people entering voluntarily, hopes to time a book critiquing the franchise to the fourth film, and recommends Blue Letter Bible for tracing each word."}]

No. I'm here as a fellow slave.", "author": "Clint Richardson", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/362c5ed8-980e-4411-881f-286be4c17848/CLINT-RICHARDSON.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The more free you believe you are, the less you turn out to be because you start believing in these institutions of freedom.", "author": "Clint Richardson", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/362c5ed8-980e-4411-881f-286be4c17848/CLINT-RICHARDSON.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The funny thing about natural law is it's super simple, but the legal system is absurdly complex with millions of codes and statutes and things.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "You've been given a person, a persona, which persona in the Latin means a mask.", "author": "Clint Richardson", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/362c5ed8-980e-4411-881f-286be4c17848/CLINT-RICHARDSON.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You never, ever, rule number one, you never teach a slave your language.
